connects_to.label: Compute a unit rate from a ratio

chain.rate.proportional.prompt: Two shops sell the same lollies. One sells a bag of 5 for $4. The other sells a bag of 12 for $10. Which bag is better value — and are you sure?
chain.rate.proportional.note: 80c vs about 83c. The bigger bag looks like the obvious deal and is not, so the guess is worth committing to and the reveal is a real surprise. Does not disclose the divide-to-compare method. Not open after activity 01.

connects_to.label: Recognise a proportional relationship as a line through the origin

chain.rate.proportional.prompt: After 2 minutes of filling, a paddling pool is 10 cm deep. After 2 weeks of growing, a seedling is 10 cm tall. One of these you can predict at double the time. The other you can't. Which is which?
chain.rate.proportional.note: Stays OPEN after activities 01-02: a student who can find a unit rate (5 cm/min, 5 cm/week) will confidently double both, which is the error. Probes whether doubling the input doubles the output - what a line through the origin means - so it opens the day on mis.proportional.line-misses-origin. No graph, origin or line named, so it does not front-load. Avoids any fixed-fee framing, which would front-load activity 04's DoL.

connects_to.label: Compute the gradient from two points

chain.linear.slope.prompt: A ramp rises 1 m over 10 m of ground. Tama says its gradient is 10. Aroha says it's 0.1. One of those numbers describes a gentle ramp and the other describes a wall. Which is which?
chain.linear.slope.note: Chain opener. Sets up mis.slope.rise-run-inverted: students engage by picturing '10 is steep'; the lesson earns why rise goes on top. Rise and run are given but not the division, so the method isn't handed over. Answered once activity 01 is done.

connects_to.label: Read the gradient from a graph, attending to axis scale

chain.linear.slope.prompt: Two fitness apps graph the same climb up Maungawhau. On one, the line looks like a cliff. On the other, it's nearly flat. Which app is lying?
chain.linear.slope.note: Neither: the axes use different scales. Sets up mis.slope.steeper-is-bigger. Needs two graphs of the same data on different axis scales (existing graph block). Fire before activity 03; stays open after 01–02, because a student who can compute a gradient still trusts the picture over the scale.

connects_to.label: Interpret the gradient as a rate of change in context, with units

chain.linear.slope.prompt: A candle is 20 cm tall when it's lit and 14 cm tall three hours later. Someone says, "Its number is 2." Is that enough to tell you when it will burn out?
chain.linear.slope.note: Sets up mis.slope.units-dropped: a bare 2 doesn't say 2 what, per what, or which way. The rate is -2 cm per hour, so it burns out in 7 more hours. The 2 is given, so the gradient calculation isn't front-loaded. Fire before activity 04 (two-points takes two activities). Hook-level ancestor of the derivative-units idea three years on.

connects_to.label: Find the perimeter of polygons, including missing side lengths

chain.measure.area-volume.prompt: A square patio is laid 4 paving stones long and 4 stones wide. Mele wants edging all the way round it. She counts the stones around the outside, gets 12, and says the edge is 12 stone-lengths long. Is she right?
chain.measure.area-volume.note: Chain opener, before activity 01. Shape: a fictional student's claim. Sets up mis.perimeter.counts-squares: each corner stone is counted once though it has two outside edges. Answer: 16 stone-lengths, 4 short, one per corner (a 4 x 4 square has 12 edge stones). Doesn't say 'add the sides' or name perimeter. Answered once activity 01 is done. No figure: students sketch a 4 x 4 square.

connects_to.label: Find the area of rectangles, squares and triangles in square units

chain.measure.area-volume.prompt: The school māra kai gets 20 m of fencing. One plan is a bed 9 m long and 1 m wide. The other is a square, 5 m by 5 m. Same fence, so the same amount of garden?
chain.measure.area-volume.note: Before activity 02. Shape: a surprising claim. Sets up mis.area.same-perimeter-same-area. Both fences are 20 m; the gardens are 9 m² and 25 m². Gives no formula and no unit; the reveal in m² also opens mis.units.area-as-linear. Open on day 2 only if activity 01's items for the shared misconception don't compare the areas of equal-perimeter rectangles. Answered once activity 02 is done. No figure.

connects_to.label: Find the area of a composite shape by decomposing it

chain.measure.area-volume.prompt: An L-shaped deck has two arms, each 2 m wide. Measured along the outside, one arm is 6 m long and the other is 5 m long. Rangi works out 6 × 2 = 12 and 5 × 2 = 10, and orders 22 m² of decking. Too much, too little, or just right?
chain.measure.area-volume.note: Before activity 03. Shape: a fictional student's wrong answer. Sets up mis.area.composite-overlap: both rectangles contain the 2 m x 2 m corner. Answer: 18 m², 4 m² too much. Stays open after activity 02: a student who can find a rectangle's area agrees with Rangi. The lesson earns splitting without overlap and the missing length (5 - 2 = 3). No figure: students sketch the L.

connects_to.label: Find the volume of cubes and cuboids in cubic units, as layers of unit cubes

chain.measure.area-volume.prompt: Two boxes. One is a cube, 40 cm long, 40 cm wide and 40 cm high. The other is 80 cm long, 20 cm wide and 40 cm high. Which one holds more?
chain.measure.area-volume.note: Before activity 04. Shape: two options. Sets up mis.volume.adds-dimensions (120 vs 140 makes the long box look bigger). Answer: the same, 64 000 cm³ (64 L) each. Open after activities 01-03: equal base areas don't yet mean equal volume until activity 04's layers. Gives no formula and no cubic unit. No figure.

connects_to.label: Classify triangles by sides and by angles

chain.geom.triangles-polygons.prompt: Draw a triangle with two sides the same length. Now turn your page so the triangle is lying on its side. Is it still the same kind of triangle?
chain.geom.triangles-polygons.note: Chain opener, before activity 01. Shape: do, then predict. Sets up mis.triangle.orientation-matters: a triangle that looks tipped over doesn't match the upright picture students hold, so many say it has changed. Doesn't name isosceles or say a triangle is classified by its sides and angles alone; the lesson earns both. Answered once activity 01's worked example classifies the same triangle in two orientations. No figure: students draw their own.

connects_to.label: Use the angle sums of a triangle (180°) and a quadrilateral (360°) to find missing angles

chain.geom.triangles-polygons.prompt: One triangle is painted across the whole school field. Another is drawn on your thumbnail. Which triangle's three angles add up to more?
chain.geom.triangles-polygons.note: Before activity 02. Shape: prediction (screened Y7 bank concept, Zan 30 Sep): the field triangle, the thumbnail triangle, or the same. Sets up mis.angles.sum-depends-on-size. Doesn't give 180° or hint that the total is fixed; the lesson establishes the sum. Answered once activity 02 shows every triangle's angles add to 180°, whatever its size. No figure needed.

connects_to.label: Use supplementary, complementary, vertical and adjacent angle relationships to find unknown angles

chain.geom.parallel-lines.prompt: Draw two long straight lines that cross, like a squashed X. Find the narrowest of the four angles. Kiri says the angle directly across from it must be the widest one, so the two balance each other out. Is she right?
chain.geom.parallel-lines.note: Chain opener, before activity 01. Shape: do, then a fictional student's claim to evaluate. Sets up mis.angles.vertical-as-supplementary: 'balance each other out' is the opposite angle treated as the partner that makes a straight line. Names no angle type and gives no number, so neither 'equal' nor 180° is front-loaded. Answered once activity 01's worked example shows vertically opposite angles are equal. No figure: students draw their own.

connects_to.label: Find angles where a transversal crosses parallel lines

chain.geom.parallel-lines.prompt: Ben rules a slanted line across two lines in his exercise book. That makes eight angles. He measures one of the sharp ones: 50°. "The book lines are parallel," he says, "so all eight are 50°." Before you measure anything: which of his eight angles do you think are 50°?
chain.geom.parallel-lines.note: Before activity 02. Shape: a fictional student's wrong answer, then a prediction (Zan 2026-10-07: predict, don't measure, so the hook stays under a minute and the rule isn't found by protractor). Sets up mis.parallel.all-equal (the given angle copied into every position). Stays open after activity 01 in part: 01 fixes the four angles at Ben's first crossing, but not which angles at the second crossing match. Answer: the four sharp angles are 50°, the four wide ones 130°. Names no corresponding, alternate or co-interior angles and gives no total. Answered once activity 02 is done. No figure: students rule a line across their own book lines, which really are parallel.
